Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

look! interjection

pointing something out

also behold, lo, lo and behold, see!, look, here he comes

classical

Plaut. Most. 382: Ecce autem iterum hīc dēposīvit caput et dormit.
Cic. Att. 2.8.1: ecce tibi nūntius puerōs vēnisse Rōmā!

Ecce!

with the nominative or a clause (in comedy also the accusative)

look! see! behold!

The everyday word. Ecce autem, “but look!”, brings in a surprise in a story; ecce tibi with a clause is the letters’ “and what do you know”; ecce mē, “here I am” (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • Ēn! — lo! see there!

    with the nominative or the accusative · also used · classical · Verg. A. 1.461: Ēn Priamus!

    (mostly in Vergil (Lewis & Short); in Plaut. and Ter. usually written em)

    Livelier than ecce, often indignant: ēn habet vim indignātiōnis (Donatus, quoted by Lewis & Short).

  • Eccum! Eccam! — look, here he is! here she is!

    from ecce eum, ecce eam; also eccōs, eccās · also used · classical · Plaut. Aul. 712: attat, eccum ipsum.; Plaut. Stich. 577: atque eccum tibi lupum in sermōne

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.)

Examples

  • Ecce autem iterum hīc dēposīvit caput et dormit. suscitā.

    Look, he’s put his head down again and is asleep. Wake him.Plaut. Most. 382

  • ecce autem geminī ā Tenedō tranquilla per alta (horrēscō referēns) immēnsīs orbibus anguēs incumbunt pelagō

    but look! two serpents from Tenedos, over the calm deep (I shudder to tell it), lean on the sea in huge coilsVerg. A. 2.203–205

  • ecce tibi nūntius puerōs vēnisse Rōmā!

    and what do you know, word that the boys have come from Rome!Cic. Att. 2.8.1

  • Ēn Priamus!

    See, there is Priam!Verg. A. 1.461

  • attat, eccum ipsum.

    Oh! look, there he is himself.Plaut. Aul. 712

See also there!, here you are, I’m here.
